---
title: "Estimates and sampling error"
subtitle: "1.2 · one simulated unit, after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024) and Walters' teaching slides"
description: "Sampling variation of a normally distributed estimate with a fixed true value and known standard error."
---

Consider an estimate equal to a fixed true value plus normally distributed sampling error. Repeated data collection
produces different estimates of the same quantity. The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of this
sampling distribution; approximately two-thirds of the estimates fall within one SE of the true value. The
simulation displays successive estimates and decomposes the most recent estimate into its true value and sampling
error. The **Draw** control generates a further observation from this distribution.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **SE .20.** Twenty estimates of a unit whose true value is .50: 12 of 20 fall within one SE (the filled dots),
  against 13.65 expected on average. The ringed latest estimate, .229, is the true value plus noise −.271.
- **200 draws.** With ten times as many draws, the count within one SE moves from 12 of 20 to 132 of 200, against 136.54
  expected, while the share expected on average stays .6827.
- **Seed 2.** The same unit with other data: this time 18 of 20 estimates fall within one SE. The count moves from one
  set of data to the next; the expected 13.65 does not.
- **SE .10.** Seed 1 again with half the SE: every estimate moves halfway toward the true value and the noise arrow
  halves to −.136, yet each draw keeps its noise in SEs (−1.36), so the count stays 12 of 20.
- **SE .05.** Halving the SE again gives the same standardised errors: the noise is −.068, and still 12 of 20 fall within one SE. The three SEs are
  those of the small, medium and large units in [Ranking noisy estimates](noisy-league.qmd).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The simulation specifies a fixed true value for one unit. Each estimate is the true value plus the SE times a draw from the normal
curve, taken from a seeded stream, so a seed always gives the same estimates. This is the model of Kline, Rose and
Walters (2024), Section III, Assumption 1 (stated before Section III.A), and talk slide 17. Walters' Mixtape slides
(pp. 5–6) set it up the same way, and the postrank theory book, ch. 2, "Teacher growth categories: evidence,
precision, and the choice of assessment", reads estimates together with their standard errors.
:::
